beats.narration_text: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. First, a correction. To let an agent work on a cluster, you do not just say, run my job. The cluster is shared, and the agent is fast and literal. You give it two short rule files first, and you point it at them.

beats.narration_text: Five terms. A rule file: a plain text file the agent reads before it acts. A hard never: a rule with no exceptions. A login node: the shared computer you land on when you connect. A Slurm job: your request for a compute node, written as a script. And fairshare: the priority you lose when you ask for more than you use.

beats.act: I · Why An Agent Needs Rules
beats.narration_text: An agent is fast, literal, and never tired. That is the good news. On a shared cluster it is also the risk. It will do exactly what you asked, as many times as you asked, and it will not feel the cost to anyone else.

beats.act: I · Why An Agent Needs Rules
beats.narration_text: Most trouble on a cluster is not hard computer science. It is work on the wrong machine. It is a request far bigger than the job. And it is a check that passes when it should fail. These are quiet failures: nothing crashes, and you find out later.

beats.narration_text: Open the file H P C dot M D and the first thing you see is not a rule. It is a short summary: what it is, why it exists, what was found, and what is not verified. Then a line that says everything below is for the agent. Then fourteen numbered sections, zero to thirteen, and an honest appendix of conflicts.

props.title: II · Walking Through HPC.md  ·  the headings, from the file
lines: # HPC.md: Rules for any agent helping a researcher use a shared HPC cluster
# Agent rules (everything below is for the agent)
## 0. Prime directive
## 1. Hard NEVERs (check this list before every command)
## 2. Before the first command
## 6. GPUs
## 9. Reproducibility: the record every job leaves behind
## 12. Slurm scripting traps and slide errors (do not copy these)
# Appendix A: Conflicts and unverified items (the honest list)

beats.narration_text: Section zero is the prime directive. The agent does the pipeline work: inspect, measure, size, check, keep records. The researcher keeps the judgment: what to spend, who gets access, and anything that cannot be undone. Look before you act. Measure before you change. Ask before you spend, delete, or share.

beats.narration_text: Section one is the list the agent checks before every command. Never run computation on a login node. Never ask for, read, or print a password or a key. Never delete without listing what will go and getting a yes. Never submit a job until you have confirmed what it asks for. Never cancel with S cancel dash u. And never invent a flag, a module, or a limit.

beats.narration_text: Notice that every never comes with a because. A rule the agent understands is a rule it can apply to a case the file never listed. And some rules are labelled house rule, because they are our judgment, not the cluster's policy.

… hits a shared scheduler. Check `squeue -u $USER` at most about once every 5 minutes **(house rule)**; use job …
| Invent a flag, module name, partition, version or quota | State what you could not confirm instead. |

beats.narration_text: Section two is before the first command. If a read-only command can answer a question, the agent runs it instead of asking you. Who am I, where am I, which groups, what is free. It asks only what only you can answer: your access, what it may submit, whether the data is restricted, and what you are trying to do.

beats.narration_text: Section four stops the agent asking for more than it needs. Is parallel even the answer? In Research Computing's own benchmark, one core took two hundred fifty seconds. Eight cores took twenty-nine. Twelve cores took thirty-three, slower than eight. Never promise that N cores is N times faster.

beats.narration_text: Section five: every script states its numbers. Partition, time, memory, cores, a name, and a log file. Time is the expected runtime plus about twenty percent, never the maximum just to be safe. And memory is computer memory, not GPU memory.

- **`--time` = expected runtime + about 20%, never above the partition maximum.** Estimate the runtime from a …
- **`--mem` is CPU RAM, not GPU memory.** Never raise `--mem` to cure a CUDA out-of-memory error.

beats.narration_text: Section six is GPUs. Never trust the allocation. A job that worked may have run on the processor with no error. So every GPU script proves the GPU is there before the expensive part: the device name, the memory, and a number that travels to the GPU and back.

beats.narration_text: Section eight is software, in order. First a module. Then conda. Then a container built on your own machine. Then a source build. And a tool like Spack only last, because each step down costs more to keep. Before installing anything, the agent checks whether a module already exists.

beats.narration_text: Section nine is the record every job leaves behind. The job and node. When it started. The git commit it ran from. The exact command, the parameters, the seeds, the inputs. The software, and the hardware it really used. Twelve items, so a stranger can rerun it.

beats.narration_text: Section ten is about being an agent on the cluster. The researcher creates and unlocks the key, never the agent. If a command prompts, hangs, or says permission denied, the agent stops and reports the exact error. It does not retry in a loop, and it never asks for a password.

beats.narration_text: And the appendix is the honest part. Where the sources disagree, the file says so and picks the safe reading. The scratch quota: fifty terabytes in the slides, twenty on the policy page. So the agent is told never to quote a number. Rules marked house rule or inferred are our judgment, not policy.

beats.narration_text: AICR differs in ways that bite. Your user name is built differently. There is no password, only a key and a certificate. The partition decides which GPU you get. Idle GPUs are cancelled automatically. And scratch is purged after thirty days, with no off-site backup.

beats.narration_text: AICR's own nevers are specific. Never run S S H add dash capital D, because it empties every key. Never source activate in a batch script, because a real job died on it. And never copy the workshop's GPU check, because it exits zero even when the GPU is missing.

beats.narration_text: Section five is a template built from flags that real completed jobs used. Every setting is stated. The environment is added to the path, not activated. And the script fails itself, on purpose, if the GPU is not visible.

python -c "import torch,sys; sys.exit(0 if torch.cuda.is_available() else 1)"   # hard-fail if CUDA …

beats.narration_text: After every batch job the agent runs jobstats, a command that exists only on AICR. Its real example: a job that asked for eight hours and ran fifty-five minutes, with the GPU eighty percent busy. The targets are written down: over seventy percent GPU use is acceptable, and under fifty is a problem.

beats.narration_text: Section eleven is lessons from real AICR runs, and they are all quiet failures. A checkpoint that loaded without error and left random weights. An input clip so quiet it produced silence. A cached file served under the same path after it was replaced. Each became a rule: prove the weights loaded, gate every input with a number, give a replaced file a new name.

beats.narration_text: And before any GPU job, the agent asks only what only you can answer. Your user name and account. Whether any data is restricted. Whether it may submit for you. And what success looks like.
